representative.title: Cortical Organoid Protocol and Calcitriol treatment V.1
representative.operation: Culture and treatment of cortical organoids
representative.methodVariant: Cortical organoid culture with calcitriol treatment
representative.evidenceStatus: metadata-verified; record-level permissive license not exposed in retrieved page
representative.selectionNote: Selected because the direct Protocols.io record exposes a specific cortical organoid title, author, publication date, DOI identifier, and a human brain-development context. It represents one tissue and differentiation variant, not the full organoid-culture category.

screened.title: Establishing Bipotential Human Lung Organoid Culture System and Differentiation to Generate Mature Alveolar and Airway Organoids
screened.reason: A specific human lung organoid system with alveolar and airway differentiation; it is a meaningful tissue variant but not interchangeable with cortical organoids.

screened.title: Protocol for Immune Cell Isolation, Organoid Generation, and Co-culture Establishment from Cryopreserved Whole Human Intestine
screened.reason: Combines intestinal organoid generation with immune-cell isolation and co-culture, so it has a materially different specimen and assay intent.

screened.title: Mouse Intestinal Organoid Culture Protocol
screened.reason: A mouse intestinal organoid variant with different tissue, organism, and differentiation context.

screened.title: Detailed Cerebral Organoid Fusion Method
screened.reason: Relevant cerebral-organoid source, but the title centers on organoid fusion rather than the selected baseline cortical culture system.

coverageGaps: Organoid culture spans materially different tissues, starting cell sources, extracellular matrices, and differentiation intents; the representative is only the cortical human variant.
Intestinal, lung, hepatic, neural, and co-culture systems need separate child-category representatives instead of being silently mixed.
The retrieved Protocols.io record page did not expose record-level license evidence, so reuse rights for this representative remain unresolved.
nextSearchSuggestions: Search separate child categories for intestinal, lung, hepatic, cerebral, and co-culture organoids.
Track tissue, starting cell source, matrix, differentiation intent, and treatment as independent variant fields.
Recheck each selected record for an explicit record-level license before any content reuse.

representative.title: Isolation of Primary Human Keratinocytes from Foreskin
representative.assay: Primary human keratinocyte isolation and culture
representative.operation: Isolation of primary keratinocytes from human foreskin tissue
representative.evidenceStatus: metadata-verified; source copyright statement indicates an exclusive license, not a clear permissive reuse license
representative.selectionNote: Selected because the direct Bio-protocol record identifies a specific human tissue source, primary cell type, author, publication date, DOI, and record-level copyright statement. It is a tissue-specific representative, not a universal dissociation protocol.

screened.title: Protocol for Primary Mouse Hepatocyte Isolation -- University of Minnesota TMCs
screened.reason: Specific mouse liver isolation variant with a different organism and tissue source.

screened.title: Isolation and Primary Cell Culture of Mouse Dorsal Root Ganglion Neurons
screened.reason: Mouse neuronal tissue and primary neuronal culture are materially different from human foreskin keratinocytes.

screened.title: Isolation of Highly Pure Primary Mouse Alveolar Epithelial Type II Cells by Flow Cytometric Cell Sorting
screened.reason: Mouse lung epithelial isolation adds flow-sorting and a distinct tissue/cell identity.

screened.title: Isolation and Primary Culture of Various Cell Types from Whole Human Endometrial Biopsies
screened.reason: Human endometrial biopsy isolation covers multiple cell types and a different specimen source.

screened.title: Primary isolation of vascular cells from murine brain for single cell sequencing
screened.reason: A murine brain vascular-cell isolation workflow with a single-cell sequencing readout context.

coverageGaps: Primary cell isolation spans different tissue sources, species, enzymes, mechanical dissociation schemes, and purification/readout intents; the representative is only the human foreskin keratinocyte variant.
Mouse hepatocytes, dorsal root ganglion neurons, lung epithelial cells, spleen mononuclear cells, and endometrial biopsy-derived cells require separate variants.
The Bio-protocol record exposes an exclusive-license statement rather than a clear CC reuse license; the record is suitable as metadata evidence but not a blanket permission to copy protocol content.
nextSearchSuggestions: Create child categories by tissue and species before comparing enzymes or mechanical dissociation methods.
Track purification and readout intent separately from the isolation operation.
Prefer records with explicit permissive license evidence when the catalog later needs reusable protocol content.

selfCheckNotes: Both assigned category IDs are present exactly once and in packet order.
Both representatives have stable HTTP(S) record URLs, source record IDs, and DOI metadata.
The packet is partial because both labels contain materially different tissue, species, matrix, differentiation, enzyme, or readout variants.

License evidence is incomplete for the Protocols.io representative and non-permissive for the Bio-protocol representative; no protocol steps, tables, figures, videos, PDFs, or long source passages were stored.

runNotes: Metadata-first collection used direct Protocols.io and Bio-protocol record pages, DOI landing pages, Crossref metadata, and Nature protocol-family records for variant comparison.

The cortical organoid page exposed title, author, publication date, DOI identifier, and a human brain-development context; the Bio-protocol keratinocyte page exposed title, author, publication date, DOI, and an exclusive-license copyright statement.
The result intentionally records explicit coverage and rights gaps instead of copying experimental instructions or treating one tissue-specific protocol as universal.
